input.strategy_title: AMD GPU (ROCm) enablement for serving and training
input.strategy_markdown:
## Problem Statement

Two strategic customers are standardizing on AMD Instinct accelerators and need
RHOAI to serve and train on ROCm. Upstream vLLM and PyTorch both publish ROCm
support, but the platform ships only CUDA runtime builds, and we have no
first-hand data on functional or performance parity for our supported model
set. Feature and performance validation requires physical AMD GPU hardware —
none exists in our CI fleet today — and upstream ROCm image cadence is
controlled by AMD and the upstream communities.

## High-Level Requirements

| ID | Priority | Requirement |
|-------|----------|-------------|
| HLR-1 | P0 | A validation campaign on physical AMD Instinct hardware establishes functional and performance parity data for vLLM serving of the supported model set, producing the go/no-go scope for productization. |
| HLR-2 | P0 | A supported vLLM ROCm serving runtime is productized for the models the validation campaign clears. |
| HLR-3 | P1 | PyTorch training on ROCm is supported for single- and multi-GPU jobs admitted through Kueue, with amd.com/gpu quota handling. |
| HLR-4 | P2 | Documentation states supported AMD hardware, driver prerequisites, and the validated model list. |

## Affected Components

- KServe
- Serving Runtimes
- Training Operator
- Distributed Workloads

## Out of Scope

- Intel Gaudi or other non-AMD accelerator families
- AMD GPU sharing/partitioning support

## Open Questions

1. Hardware access: the validation campaign (HLR-1) needs dedicated AMD
   Instinct nodes — procurement or partner-lab access is unresolved.
2. Upstream ROCm build cadence: whether AMD's runtime image releases align
   with our release trains is outside our control.

# AMD Instinct vLLM serving validation campaign (functional/performance parity, go/no-go)

## Description

This epic resolves the central unknown of the AMD GPU (ROCm) enablement
strategy: whether vLLM serving on AMD Instinct accelerators achieves
functional and performance parity with the platform's CUDA-based vLLM runtime
for the supported model set. It runs a validation campaign on physical AMD
Instinct hardware, produces first-hand functional and performance parity data
per model, and delivers the go/no-go recommendation that bounds the scope of
the vLLM ROCm serving-runtime productization work.

## Scope

- Secure access to dedicated AMD Instinct GPU nodes (procurement or partner-lab
  access) — the epic's work includes securing access; the timing of external
  granting is a risk, not a deliverable condition.
- Define the validation campaign methodology: the supported model set under
  test, functional pass/fail criteria per model, and performance parity
  measurement methodology against the CUDA baseline.
- Execute the campaign: run vLLM serving of the supported model set on ROCm on
  the AMD Instinct nodes, collecting functional results and performance
  metrics per model.
- Produce the validation report: per-model functional pass/fail, performance
  parity data, and the go/no-go recommendation with the list of models cleared
  for productization.
- Record driver and ROCm runtime versions used, so the productization and
  documentation work can reference validated configurations.

## Acceptance Criteria

- The validation campaign plan is documented and covers every model in the
  supported model set, with a defined functional pass/fail criterion and a
  defined performance parity measurement for each.
- Functional results exist for every model in the supported model set: each
  model is marked pass or fail against its criterion.
- Performance parity data is captured for every functionally passing model,
  measured against the CUDA vLLM baseline under the documented methodology.
- The validation report is published and states, per model: functional result,
  performance parity data, and driver/ROCm runtime versions used.
- The report delivers a go/no-go recommendation enumerating the models cleared
  for productization (the list may be empty, partial, or complete — the
  deliverable is the decision data, not a particular outcome).

## HLR Traceability

- HLR-1 (P0): A validation campaign on physical AMD Instinct hardware
  establishes functional and performance parity data for vLLM serving of the
  supported model set, producing the go/no-go scope for productization.

## Risks / Notes

- Hardware access is an availability precondition controlled by parties
  outside the strategy (procurement or partner-lab negotiation); its timing
  cannot be compressed by engineering effort and gates campaign execution.
- Upstream ROCm runtime image cadence is controlled by AMD and upstream
  communities; the campaign should pin and record the versions it validates.

# Productize vLLM ROCm serving runtime for validated models

## Description

This epic productizes a supported vLLM ROCm serving runtime for the models
cleared by the AMD Instinct validation campaign, extending the platform's
Serving Runtimes portfolio (currently CUDA-only) with an AMD Instinct
variant. The runtime must be deployable through the existing KServe
InferenceService machinery and built through the existing runtime build and
release pipeline.

## Scope

- Build and productize vLLM ROCm runtime images for the models cleared by the
  validation campaign, based on the ROCm baseline validated in the campaign.
- Define and ship the ServingRuntime/ClusterServingRuntime resources that make
  the ROCm vLLM runtime selectable for inference on AMD Instinct nodes.
- Ensure the runtime integrates with accelerator discovery on AMD GPU nodes so
  InferenceServices using this runtime schedule onto AMD Instinct nodes.
- Validate deployment through KServe InferenceServices (serverless and/or raw
  deployment mode as supported) without KServe code changes — KServe
  compatibility is verified here, not modified.
- Align the runtime's ROCm image baseline with platform release trains,
  subject to upstream ROCm image availability.

## Acceptance Criteria

- A vLLM ROCm serving runtime image builds successfully through the existing
  runtime build pipeline (pipeline green) for every model on the campaign's
  cleared list.
- The runtime is selectable via ServingRuntime resources and serves every
  cleared model with functional behavior matching the campaign's validated
  results.
- An InferenceService using the ROCm vLLM runtime deploys and serves on AMD
  Instinct nodes through existing KServe machinery, with no KServe code
  changes required (KServe is validated as-is).
- The runtime's ROCm image baseline and driver prerequisites are recorded and
  consistent with the versions the validation campaign certified.
- The scope of productized models exactly matches the campaign's cleared-model
  list; models that did not clear are documented as unsupported on ROCm.

## HLR Traceability

- HLR-2 (P0): A supported vLLM ROCm serving runtime is productized for the
  models the validation campaign clears.

## Risks / Notes

- Scope is bounded by the validation campaign's go/no-go outcome: the cleared
  model list (partial, complete, or empty) rewrites this epic's scope, not its
  structure.
- Upstream ROCm runtime image release cadence is controlled by AMD and the
  upstream communities and may not align with platform release trains; this is
  a timing risk on the image baseline chosen, not a change in what is built.

# Kueue amd.com/gpu quota handling and admission for ROCm workloads

## Description

This epic enables the Distributed Workloads stack's queueing layer to admit
workloads requesting AMD Instinct GPUs: `amd.com/gpu` resource quota handling
in the Kueue ClusterQueue/LocalQueue model, and all-or-nothing (gang)
admission of multi-GPU ROCm jobs onto AMD GPU nodes.

## Scope

- Extend the quota/admission configuration model of the Distributed Workloads
  stack so ClusterQueues/LocalQueues can meter and limit `amd.com/gpu`
  resources, mirroring how NVIDIA GPU quota is handled today.
- Ensure resource flavors can target AMD Instinct node pools so queued
  workloads requesting `amd.com/gpu` admit onto the right nodes.
- Verify all-or-nothing admission (gang semantics via waitForPodsReady) for
  multi-GPU and multi-node ROCm job topologies.
- Validate admission behavior with representative queued workloads requesting
  `amd.com/gpu` (single-GPU and multi-GPU), including quota exhaustion and
  queueing behavior.

## Acceptance Criteria

- A ClusterQueue/LocalQueue configuration meters and enforces quota on
  `amd.com/gpu`, and workloads exceeding quota remain pending rather than
  admitting.
- Workloads requesting `amd.com/gpu` are admitted onto AMD Instinct node
  pools, with correct resource accounting per admitted workload.
- Multi-GPU/multi-node ROCm job topologies admit all-or-nothing: partial
  topologies do not admit, and released quota is reclaimed when workloads
  finish.
- Admission validation results for single- and multi-GPU ROCm workloads are
  documented, including quota-exhaustion and queueing behavior.

## HLR Traceability

- HLR-3 (P1, shared): PyTorch training on ROCm is supported for single- and
  multi-GPU jobs admitted through Kueue, with amd.com/gpu quota handling —
  this epic delivers the quota/admission half.

## Risks / Notes

- On-hardware admission validation requires AMD Instinct nodes; where
  hardware access is shared with the serving validation campaign, coordinate
  scheduling — hardware availability is an external precondition, not a
  deliverable condition.

# PyTorchJob ROCm training support (single- and multi-GPU)

## Description

This epic makes PyTorch distributed training on AMD Instinct GPUs a supported
path: PyTorchJob workloads running ROCm-based PyTorch training images, in
single- and multi-GPU topologies, admitted through Kueue with `amd.com/gpu`
quota handling.

## Scope

- Enable PyTorchJob workers to run ROCm-based PyTorch training images on AMD
  Instinct nodes, including the worker/launcher configuration needed for
  single-GPU and multi-GPU (multi-node) topologies.
- Validate end-to-end training: PyTorchJobs admitted through Kueue queues
  configured for `amd.com/gpu`, executing training runs on ROCm — the quota
  configuration itself is delivered by the Distributed Workloads stack and is
  consumed here as a configuration reference, not rebuilt.
- Document validated PyTorch ROCm image baselines and job configuration
  patterns for single- and multi-GPU training.
- Capture validation results (functional training runs, scaling behavior
  across single/multi-GPU) on AMD Instinct hardware.

## Acceptance Criteria

- A single-GPU PyTorchJob running a ROCm PyTorch training image completes a
  training run on an AMD Instinct node, admitted through a Kueue queue
  metering `amd.com/gpu`.
- A multi-GPU PyTorchJob (multi-worker and/or multi-GPU-per-worker topology)
  completes a distributed training run on AMD Instinct nodes with the same
  admission path.
- End-to-end validation is performed against Kueue queues configured for
  `amd.com/gpu` (the quota configuration is available as a configuration
  reference at validation time — no rebuild of quota handling in this epic).
- Validated PyTorch ROCm image baselines and job configuration patterns are
  documented, with driver/ROCm versions recorded.

## HLR Traceability

- HLR-3 (P1, shared): PyTorch training on ROCm is supported for single- and
  multi-GPU jobs admitted through Kueue, with amd.com/gpu quota handling —
  this epic delivers the PyTorchJob training half.

## Risks / Notes

- Validation requires AMD Instinct nodes; where hardware access is shared with
  the serving validation campaign, coordinate scheduling — hardware
  availability is an external precondition, not a deliverable condition.
- Upstream PyTorch ROCm image cadence is controlled by upstream communities
  and AMD; the image baseline to validate against is a timing risk, not a
  change in what is built.

# Document AMD hardware support, driver prerequisites, and validated model list

## Description

This epic authors the customer-facing documentation for AMD GPU (ROCm)
enablement: the supported AMD Instinct hardware, driver prerequisites, and the
validated model list for vLLM ROCm serving (plus the validated PyTorch ROCm
training configuration), reflecting what was actually built and validated.

## Scope

- Supported AMD Instinct accelerators and the hardware requirements for both
  serving and training on ROCm.
- Driver and ROCm runtime prerequisites, including the validated driver/ROCm
  versions recorded by the validation campaign and productization work.
- The validated model list for vLLM ROCm serving — exactly the models the
  validation campaign cleared and the productized runtime supports — with
  models that did not clear explicitly documented as unsupported on ROCm.
- How to run PyTorch training on ROCm: single- and multi-GPU PyTorchJobs
  admitted through Kueue with `amd.com/gpu` quota, using the validated job
  configuration patterns.
- Scope boundaries carried over from the strategy: non-AMD accelerator
  families and AMD GPU sharing/partitioning are out of scope and documented as
  unsupported.

## Acceptance Criteria

- Documentation topics covering supported AMD hardware, driver prerequisites,
  the validated model list for serving, and ROCm training configuration are
  authored and published through the Red Hat docs content process.
- The documented validated model list matches the productized runtime's
  supported model set exactly.
- The documented driver/ROCm prerequisites match the versions validated on
  hardware and shipped in the productized runtime.
- All content is technically reviewed against the implemented and validated
  behavior (reviewed by the owning engineers of the serving runtime and
  training stack).

## HLR Traceability

- HLR-4 (P2): Documentation states supported AMD hardware, driver
  prerequisites, and the validated model list.

## Risks / Notes

- Documentation content depends on the outcomes of the validation campaign,
  runtime productization, and training enablement; it is scheduled after all
  implementation work by design.
- Epic priority is P1 via the docs-authoring priority exception (strategy
  frontmatter `priority: Major` → P1); the HLR's P2 label reads as relative
  value, not a deferral signal.
